name: Wagogo nindo and cipande polyphony (Tanzania)
lineage: Wagogo polyphonic singing tradition of central Tanzania (Dodoma region), one of sub-Saharan Africa's most structurally distinctive choral traditions. Multi-part harmony built on overlapping ostinato pattern-cycles with characteristic diaphonic-and-triadic intervals — nindo work-songs and msunyunho ritual songs sit alongside the cipande circumcision-initiation repertoire. Polo Vallejo's 1995-2002 fieldwork in Nzali village (published as Mbudi Mbudi na Mhanga, Madrid 2004) and David Fanshawe's 1969-1975 East African field recordings (Saydisc CMIL 98 Fabulous Gogo Music) constitute the canonical documentation. Performance involves women's choral antiphonal patterns over zeze board-zither and kebero drum accompaniment, with characteristic call-and-response between soloist and group across staggered melodic entries. Modal vocabulary draws on pentatonic-and-hexatonic frameworks with characteristic equiheptatonic-leaning inflections distinct from neighboring Bantu traditions. Distinguished from Burundi inanga-chuchotée by Wagogo's open-voiced choral-with-instruments configuration; distinguished from Aka and Baka pygmy polyphony by Wagogo's ostinato-cycle (vs hocketed yodel) architecture; distinguished from Maasai and Sukuma neighbors by Wagogo-Dodoma dialect-specific cadential conventions.
